title: Homework & Self-Study

pts: The best homework consolidates or extends class work rather than mechanically repeating the same exercise type.
Repetition without added value or context quickly becomes a compliance task rather than a learning one.
Ask what this homework adds that the class time didn't already cover.

items: Take an exercise done in class (for example, sentences about daily routines).
Instead of more of the same, set a task that uses the language in a new way: Interview one family member about their day and write five sentences.
Learners share one sentence at the start of the next lesson.
Collect a few examples for a class display.
Photo homework: take or draw a picture and write two sentences about it.
Teach it: explain today’s grammar point to a younger sibling (in any language) and write what they said.
Support: a sentence frame.
Stretch: interview two people and compare.

lines: Repeat: Do exercises 7–12 on page 34. (same as class)
Extend: Ask your grandmother what she did every day when she was your age. Write five sentences with used to.

body: Purpose: to contrast homework types. Content: two arrows from a box labelled ‘class lesson’. One arrow loops back into the same box (‘repeat’). The other leads forward into a house with a family, labelled ‘extend: new context’. Style: simple, warm. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Classroom (free). Post the task; learners with access upload a photo of their written work.

blocks.x: Written in notebooks and shared orally in the next lesson.

points.sub: Same discipline as a lesson aim
pts: Every homework task should tie to a specific aim, the same discipline Unit 9 applies to in-class activities.
Homework assigned out of habit, without a clear aim, is the first thing learners learn to deprioritise.
State the aim to learners explicitly — purpose visible to the learner increases completion rates.

items: When setting homework, state the aim in one sentence: This will help you remember today’s words.
Write the aim beside the task on the board.
Learners copy both into their diaries.
In the next lesson, ask: Did it help?
Learners suggest the aim themselves.
Not applicable (whole-class routine).

lines: This will help you use the past tense without looking at the board.
This will help you speak about your family for one minute.

body: Purpose: to show homework framing. Content: a diary page with two lines: ‘Task: Write five sentences about your grandmother’s childhood.’ and ‘Why: to practise used to in real sentences.’ The ‘Why’ line is highlighted. Style: realistic diary page. Board version: two lines on the board.

items: Google Classroom or a class WhatsApp group (with school permission) for posting task and aim.

pts: Design homework around learners' actual available time and access to materials, not an idealised study schedule.
Overambitious homework loads reliably produce partial or no completion, undermining the whole system's credibility.
A smaller, consistently completed task beats a larger, frequently skipped one.

items: Ask learners (anonymously) how much time they usually have for English homework.
Design tasks that most learners can complete in fifteen to twenty minutes.
Avoid tasks that need materials or help that some learners do not have.
Offer a choice of two tasks where possible.
Check completion rates and adjust.
Weekend tasks slightly longer; weekday tasks shorter.
Support: shorter version for learners with heavy home responsibilities.
Stretch: an optional extension for those with more time.

lines: Does the task need a device? If yes, is there an offline version?
Does it need an English-speaking adult? If yes, change it.
Can most learners finish in about fifteen minutes?

body: Purpose: to show homework in a real day. Content: a timeline of a learner’s afternoon and evening: travel home, chores, meal, sibling care, homework for several subjects. A small green slot labelled ‘English: 15 min’. Style: clean, sympathetic. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free), anonymous, for the time survey.

body: A short task that almost everyone completes is worth more than a long task that only a few do properly. Completion builds the habit, and the habit is what matters over a year.

pts: Short, spaced homework tasks across several days outperform one large task completed the night before it's due.
This directly extends Unit 5's forgetting-curve principle from vocabulary recycling to overall homework design.
Where possible, structure a week's homework as several small touchpoints rather than one large block.

items: Replace one large weekly task with five small daily tasks.
Each task takes about five minutes: review five words, write two sentences, read one page, say one thing aloud.
Learners tick each day on a card.
Collect cards weekly; celebrate complete weeks.
Include items from previous weeks (spacing).
Pair ‘study buddies’ check each other’s cards.
Support: three tasks a week instead of five.
Stretch: add a sixth optional task.

lines: Mon: test yourself on five new words. Tue: write two sentences using them. Wed: read one page of your class reader. Thu: test yourself on last week’s words. Fri: tell someone at home one thing you learned in English.

body: Purpose: a photocopiable card. Content: a small card with five rows (Mon–Fri), a task per row and a tick box, plus a space for a parent’s or learner’s signature. Style: clean, cheerful. Board version: not applicable.

items: Quizlet or Anki (free versions) for daily self-testing.

blocks.x: The paper card and paper flashcards.

points.sub: Teach how to study, not just what
pts: Teach learners how to study independently — using dictionaries, apps, extensive reading — rather than assuming they already know how.
Strategy training pays off across the whole course, not just for one assignment.
This connects to the autonomy-readiness assessment from Unit 2 — training should match, and can raise, that readiness.

items: Demonstrate three study strategies: self-testing with flashcards, looking a word up in a dictionary (all the information), and reading with a question in mind.
Learners practise each in class for five minutes.
Each learner chooses one strategy for homework this week.
Next lesson, learners report what they did and whether it helped.
Invite older learners to demonstrate strategies they use.
Support: step-by-step strategy cards.
Stretch: learners compare two strategies and report.

blocks.x: Using a dictionary fully: for borrow, learners note pronunciation, meaning, the pattern borrow something from someone, the opposite lend, and an example sentence.

body: Purpose: photocopiable strategy prompts. Content: three small cards with an icon and three short steps each: ‘Test yourself’ (flashcard icon), ‘Dictionary detective’ (magnifying glass), ‘Read with a question’ (question mark). Style: consistent card design. Board version: not applicable.

items: Cambridge Dictionary or Oxford Learner’s Dictionaries online (free).

blocks.x: A paper learner’s dictionary per bench.

pts: Homework without any feedback loop quickly loses value in learners' eyes, whatever its content.
Even brief acknowledgment — a quick check, a comment, a show of hands on difficulty — sustains the habit of doing it.
Feedback here can be lightweight; the key variable is that it exists at all.

v: 2–5 minutes at the start of a lesson

items: At the start of the lesson, learners compare homework with a partner.
Ask two or three learners to share an answer or sentence.
Collect one quick signal: fingers for how hard it was.
Mark a sample of homework in detail (a row each lesson).
Say something about the homework every time, so learners know it matters.
A short quiz based on the homework.
Support: partner helps complete missing parts.
Stretch: learners explain an answer to the class.

lines: Hold up your notebooks… Good. Tell your partner your best sentence. Priya, what’s yours? Lovely. And that used to is exactly right.

body: Purpose: to show homework feedback as a cycle. Content: a circle: ‘set with a reason’ → ‘learners do it’ → ‘quick check in class’ → ‘teacher uses what she sees’ → back to ‘set’. Style: clean cycle. Board version: four words in a circle.

items: Google Forms (free) for a two-question homework check where devices are available.

blocks.x: Partner checks and a show of fingers.

pts: Graded readers assigned as homework build vocabulary and fluency with minimal teacher marking load.
This combines Unit 3's extensive-reading principle with Unit 5's vocabulary depth work, largely self-sustaining once set up.
Track completion lightly (a reading log) rather than demanding heavy comprehension marking for every book.

items: Set extensive reading as the default homework on two or three days a week.
Learners choose easy books from the class library (Unit 3, Unit 31).
They record title, pages and a one-word reaction in their log.
Once a week, learners tell a partner about their book in two minutes.
Do not test comprehension of individual books.
Share books between classes to widen choice.
Support: picture books and very short stories.
Stretch: learners write a short review.

lines: 14 Sept / The Clever Crow / pages 1–12 / funny

body: Purpose: a photocopiable log. Content: a page with columns for date, title, pages, and a small face to circle. At the bottom, a bar to colour for every ten pages read. Style: friendly, simple. Board version: not applicable.

items: StoryWeaver (free) for learners with access.

blocks.x: Class library box; books taken home in a cloth bag.

body: Extensive reading is one of the few homework tasks that needs almost no marking and still produces strong gains in vocabulary and fluency over time (Day and Bamford 1998). Its cost is in building the library, not in the teacher’s evenings.

points.sub: Match the load to the learner
pts: Calibrate the amount of self-directed homework to the autonomy readiness assessed in Unit 2.
A learner not yet ready for open-ended self-study needs more structured tasks, not less homework altogether.
Autonomy can be built gradually through homework design itself, not just assumed as a fixed starting trait.

items: Offer a menu of three tasks at different levels of independence: a set exercise, a guided task, an open project.
Learners choose one each week.
Encourage learners gradually to move towards more open tasks.
Review choices with learners each month.
Let learners propose their own homework task for teacher approval.
Support: the set exercise.
Stretch: the open project.

lines: B (guided): Write a short email to a friend using five words from today.
C (open): Find an English video about a topic you like and tell the class three things you learned.

body: Purpose: to show choice by independence. Content: a café-style menu card listing three ‘dishes’: ‘Structured’, ‘Guided’, ‘Open’, each with a short description and a small icon. Style: playful menu design. Board version: three options on the board.

items: Google Classroom (free) with three task options.

blocks.x: Menu written on the board each Monday.

body: Offer a homework menu for four weeks. Record which option each learner chooses. Do learners move towards more independent options over time? That movement is evidence of growing autonomy (Unit 48).

dek: Unit 19 of 100: designing what happens between classes — purposeful, spaced, and calibrated to how much independence a given learner is actually ready for.

aims.x: This unit is about the learning that happens between lessons. It shows how to design homework that extends class work, fits learners’ real lives, uses spacing well and teaches learners how to study on their own.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: design homework that extends rather than repeats class work;
link each homework task to a clear aim;
set tasks that are feasible for learners’ real circumstances;
structure homework as spaced practice;
teach self-study strategies explicitly;
close the feedback loop on homework efficiently;
use extensive reading as low-marking, high-value homework;
match the amount of self-directed work to learners’ autonomy.

why: Why this matters. Class time alone rarely reaches the exposure and practice volume language learning needs. Well-designed homework is where that gap gets closed.

background.x: Class time is short. Four or five periods a week, minus assemblies, examinations and holidays, may add up to well under a hundred hours of English a year. Language learning needs far more exposure and practice than that. Homework and self-study are how the gap is filled, or left open.

Research on homework in general education gives a mixed but useful picture. Harris Cooper and colleagues’ synthesis (2006) found a positive relationship between homework and achievement, stronger for older students than younger ones, and suggested that more is not always better. For language learning specifically, the value of homework depends heavily on its design: short, regular, purposeful tasks tend to help; long, repetitive, unchecked ones tend to be copied, skipped or resented.

Two findings from memory research are especially relevant. The first is that practice spread over time is more effective than practice massed together (Cepeda et al. 2006). The second is that retrieving information, by testing oneself, strengthens memory more than rereading it (Dunlosky et al. 2013). Both suggest that small, frequent homework tasks involving recall are better than a single large task before a test.

Homework also exists in real homes. Some learners share a room with siblings, help with household work, travel long distances or have no one at home who reads English. Good homework design takes these realities seriously, which is a matter of fairness as well as effectiveness.

items: Completion rate. Track the proportion of learners completing homework weekly and adjust task size.
Spaced recall. Test words set as daily homework after one and four weeks.
Strategy use. Ask learners which strategy they used and check notebooks.
Reading volume. Count pages read per learner per month.
What homework did you set last week? What did it add to the lesson?
How long does your homework actually take learners? How do you know?
How do you acknowledge homework when learners bring it?
Which learners rarely complete homework? What might be stopping them?
How could extensive reading replace some of the homework you set now?

terms.def: Reading large quantities of easy, self-selected material for pleasure and general understanding, such as graded readers or StoryWeaver books (Day and Bamford 1998). It builds fluency, vocabulary and reading habits.
A cycle in which feedback leads to action and the result is checked, for example comment, revision and review. Without closing the loop, feedback on homework or writing has little effect.
Work learners do outside class. Well-designed homework extends class work, fits learners’ real circumstances, uses spaced practice and teaches independent study habits.
A set of homework options at different levels of independence, such as a structured exercise, a guided writing task and an open project, from which learners choose.

The capacity to take charge of one’s own learning, including setting goals, choosing materials and methods, and evaluating progress (Holec 1981); it is developed gradually, through guided choices, rather than simply handed over.

A simple record in which learners note what they have read, for how long and a brief response. It supports extensive reading and self-study, and helps the teacher monitor quantity and enjoyment without formal testing.

Learning by actively recalling information from memory, for example through self-quizzing or flashcards, rather than rereading it. Retrieval strengthens long-term retention (Roediger and Karpicke 2006), especially when spread over time.

Learning that learners do on their own outside class, such as reading, listening, vocabulary review or practice with apps. With limited class hours in most Indian schools, well-taught self-study strategies greatly extend learning time.

Spreading study or practice over several sessions with gaps between them, rather than concentrating it in one block. Spaced practice leads to better long-term retention than cramming the night before an examination.

A deliberate technique learners use to learn more effectively on their own, such as retrieval practice, spaced review, keeping a vocabulary notebook or planning study time. Such strategies need to be taught explicitly.
